domain: International Humanitarian Law / Law of Armed Conflict
topic_summary: Analysis of combatant status definitions under the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols, examining how different interpretative frameworks produce divergent constraints on detention, targeting, and treatment of fighters in conventional versus asymmetric warfare contexts.

key_entities: Geneva Conventions 1949 (treaty framework establishing IHL protections)
Additional Protocol I 1977 (extending protections to wars of national liberation)
Additional Protocol II 1977 (governing non-international armed conflicts)
State military forces (conventional armies with clear command structure)
Non-state armed groups (insurgents, liberation movements, organized militias)
Unlawful combatants / unprivileged belligerents (category disputed by some states)
key_tensions: State sovereignty vs insurgent legitimacy (who gets POW status and immunity from prosecution)
Distinction principle vs civilian immunity (how combatant definition affects targeting rules)
Treaty universality vs selective implementation (state vs non-state actor obligations)
key_mechanisms: Article 4 POW status criteria (fixed characteristics: command, insignia, arms openly, laws of war)
Common Article 3 baseline protections (minimum standards for all parties in non-international conflicts)
key_absences: Explicit status for cyber combatants or autonomous weapon operators
Resolution mechanism for contested status determinations in occupation scenarios

axes.structural_delta: Combatant status granted only to state-organized forces meeting Article 4 criteria; non-state fighters categorically excluded from POW protections
axes.primary_observable: State practice in detention policy; domestic prosecution rates of captured insurgents
axes.selection_reason: Primary reading with highest structural extractiveness; establishes baseline constraint against which other readings diverge

axes.structural_delta: Combatant status extended to organized armed groups fighting colonial domination, foreign occupation, or racist regimes under AP I Article 1(4)
axes.primary_observable: AP I ratification patterns; state recognition of liberation movements as legitimate belligerents
axes.selection_reason: Structurally distinct reading with different beneficiary/victim topology and different treaty substrate (AP I)

axes.structural_delta: All detained persons receive Common Article 3 protections regardless of combatant status; detention and trial rights delinked from POW classification
axes.primary_observable: Judicial interpretations (ICJ, ICTY); human rights treaty application in armed conflict
axes.selection_reason: Third structural position representing humanitarian minimum distinct from both state-centric and liberation frameworks

axes.structural_delta: Third category below civilian and combatant; fighters not meeting Article 4 criteria receive neither POW protections nor civilian immunities
axes.primary_observable: U.S. detention practice post-9/11; Guantanamo legal framework
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: overlaps structurally with state_centric_reading victim topology; adds extractiveness but not structural novelty

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Third status category denying both POW and civilian protections
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Structural overlap with state_centric_reading victim topology; represents intensification rather than independent axis

omegas.description: Geneva framework silent on cyber operators and autonomous systems. Do remote drone operators qualify as combatants? Does AI targeting software? Absence leaves constraint undefined for emerging warfare modes.
No neutral arbiter specified when parties contest combatant status. ICRC opinion is advisory; domestic courts defer to executive. Gap enables extractive framing without accountability.

Major powers (U.S., Israel, India, Pakistan, Iran, Turkey) have not ratified AP I. National liberation reading has formal treaty status but limited binding authority. Constraint exists legally but not operationally for non-parties.
omegas.source: Extraction phase recognition of AP I ratification gap

omegas.description: Three readings selected for generation coexist in international practice (state_centric in conventional wars, national_liberation in decolonization conflicts, functional_protection as judicial minimum). This is licensed plurality, not collapse. No single state applies all three consistently, but all three are live interpretive positions.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Domain is well within model training coverage (IHL is extensively documented). Three readings are structurally independent with different beneficiary/victim topologies and different ε profiles.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Geneva Conventions Articles 4 and 5 on combatant status criteria (command structure, fixed distinctive sign, carrying arms openly, conducting operations per laws of war)
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Treaty text interpreted by state practice, ICRC commentary, and international tribunals; no centralized enforcement
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Authority Capture (state parties control interpretation via selective ratification and domestic implementation)

readings.commitment: Combatant status requires formal state military organization meeting Article 4 criteria; non-state actors categorically excluded from POW protections
readings.authority_grounding: Traditional state-sovereignty interpretation; pre-AP I treaty framework
readings.expected_structural_delta: High ε for non-state fighters (no POW immunity, subject to prosecution under domestic law); low ε for state militaries (full Geneva protections)

readings.commitment: Combatant status extends to non-state armed groups fighting colonial/occupation/racist regimes under AP I Article 1(4) if organized and command-controlled
readings.authority_grounding: Additional Protocol I (1977) treaty text; ICRC interpretation; decolonization-era state practice
readings.expected_structural_delta: Mod ε for liberation movements (conditional POW status if criteria met); high ε for occupying powers (obligation to grant combatant immunity to insurgents)

readings.commitment: All detained persons receive Common Article 3 minimum protections regardless of combatant status; humane treatment and fair trial rights are status-independent
readings.authority_grounding: Judicial interpretation (ICJ, ICTY); human rights law convergence with IHL; ICRC customary law study
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low ε for all detainees (baseline floor of protections applies universally); removes status determination as precondition for humane treatment

axiom_contradictions.basis: State-centric axiom holds that combatant privilege flows exclusively from state authorization; national liberation axiom holds that combatant privilege can flow from resistance to illegitimate state authority. No coherent framework grants both: either state authority is necessary for combatant status (state-centric) or resistance to state authority can ground combatant status (liberation). These are mutually exclusive foundational commitments about the source of legitimate violence.
